A person raising this to consensus supplies two citations by different authors.

explanation: The prisoners shot in April and May 1940 were taken in September 1939, when the Soviet Union occupied eastern Poland — the half the pact's secret protocol of 23 August had assigned it. Without that protocol there is no Soviet advance into Poland that autumn, and without the advance the NKVD is not holding twenty-two thousand Polish officers, policemen and officials to shoot. The edge is `enabled` rather than `caused` because the pact says nothing about what to do with prisoners: the order of March 1940 was Stalin's and Beria's, and the reasoning behind it — removing the officer class of a state the two signatories had agreed to abolish — belongs to Soviet policy and not to the treaty. What the treaty did was put those men in Soviet hands, which is the sense in which it is a condition of the massacre and not its cause.
